expected_output.reasoning:
The expected root cause describes a customer-side cause (not an AWS-side problem) — the investigation should distinguish real causes (expired credential, quota change, invalid model ID, config change) with evidence rather than assuming an AWS outage, and should correctly attribute errors to the actual workloads causing them without conflating unrelated seeded-fault workloads.

The investigation does exactly this: it determines this is NOT an AWS problem but a customer-side issue. It identifies two distinct, evidence-backed root causes for the steady-rate errors: (1) the support agent configured with a nonexistent model ID (us.amazon.nova-micro-v9:0) causing ValidationException, and (2) the billing agent's IAM role lacking bedrock:InvokeModel permission causing AccessDeniedException — both tied to specific CloudTrail/config evidence (timestamps, role ARNs, policy details). It also correctly separates out the unrelated 13:45-14:15 burst as deliberate fault-injection test apps (llmops-lf-*), explicitly noting "These are expected test errors, not a production fault" — exactly matching the expectation that unrelated seeded-fault workloads' errors should not be attributed to the real issue. The investigation also flags gaps/unconfirmed items rather than overclaiming.

This matches the expected root cause pattern closely: identifying an invalid model ID and a missing IAM permission as the real customer-side causes, while explicitly distinguishing them from unrelated eval/demo noise, and ruling out an AWS-side problem.
